100.s: Black Sea spillover has reached its waters.
i: Likely Russian drones struck two civilian ships in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on 12–13 October.
Ships carrying Ukrainian grain have been sunk, raising freight and insurance costs.
Frequent elections and fragile coalitions slow decision-making.
100.b: Black Sea shipping risk raises insurance and freight costs for ports and traders.

104.s: Civil war continues after a military-run election.
i: Resistance forces and ethnic armed groups still contest large areas.
Polls held under the junta have not ended the conflict or won broad acceptance.
Industrial-scale online fraud along the borders draws regional crackdowns.
104.b: Civil war, sanctions and scam-centre crime make most commercial activity high risk.

112.s: A Russian staging ground facing tight Western sanctions.
i: Russian forces and tactical nuclear weapons stationed in Belarus raise NATO concern.
Western sanctions restrict trade, finance and transport links.
Migration pressure and incidents with Poland and Lithuania keep borders tense.
112.b: Western sanctions make doing business in Belarus legally risky for most international firms.

124.s: Stable, with trade friction with the US.
i: Tariffs on steel, aluminium and autos hurt exporters.
The 2026 review could reshape market access.
Competition in the Arctic is rising.
124.b: US tariffs and the USMCA review create uncertainty for autos, steel, aluminium and cross-border supply chains.

148.s: Absorbing the spillover from Sudan’s war.
i: Hundreds of thousands of refugees have crossed into eastern Chad.
Power is concentrated around President Mahamat Déby.
Jihadist groups remain active in the west.
148.b: Insecurity and refugee pressure limit operations to the capital and the oil sector.

156.s: Strategic rivalry with the US, pressure on Taiwan and a slowing economy.
i: Large-scale military activity around Taiwan keeps the risk of a crisis present.
Export controls and the AI race drive decoupling in semiconductors.
Property weakness and soft demand weigh on growth.
156.b: Export controls, tariffs and Taiwan risk push firms to diversify supply chains away from China.

158.s: The world’s most consequential flashpoint for supply chains.
i: Monthly air incursions are lower than in 2024–25, but China massed a near-90-ship fleet around the island in August.
About $29.7 billion in US weapons sold to Taiwan had not been delivered as of June.
Taiwan makes roughly 90% of the world’s most advanced chips, so any disruption is global.
158.b: Any disruption would hit global semiconductor supply chains.
sc: Coercion short of conflict: PLA patrols and drills continue, with periodic large exercises around the island.
A blockade-style quarantine or major crisis that disrupts shipping and chip exports.
A quieter period as US and Chinese leaders seek stability around the APEC meeting in Shenzhen.

170.s: A new government faces armed groups and strained US ties.
i: The ELN and FARC dissident factions have expanded their reach.
Disputes over drug policy have strained cooperation.
The administration inaugurated on 7 August is setting its security agenda.
170.b: Armed groups threaten mining, oil and rural logistics, and US–Colombia tension adds trade risk.

180.s: War in the east despite peace deals.
i: Rwanda-backed M23 still holds Goma and Bukavu.
US- and Qatar-brokered agreements have not ended the fighting.
Cobalt and coltan deals with the US raise stakes and governance risk.
180.b: Cobalt and coltan supply chains face conflict, smuggling and due diligence risks.

192.s: Energy collapse and growing pressure from Washington.
i: The end of Venezuelan oil shipments has deepened fuel shortages and blackouts.
President Trump revived the idea of military intervention at a rally on 23 October.
192.b: Blackouts, fuel shortages and US sanctions make commercial activity extremely difficult.

218.s: Gang violence tied to the cocaine trade.
i: Homicide rates are among the highest in Latin America.
Gangs run prisons, and emergency rule is frequent.
218.b: Gang violence and extortion threaten logistics, ports and banana and shrimp exporters.

231.s: Internal insurgencies and tension with Eritrea.
i: Fano militias still contest much of the Amhara region.
Rhetoric over Red Sea access has raised the risk of interstate war.
Splits within Tigrayan leadership threaten the 2022 deal.
231.b: Conflict in Amhara and tension with Eritrea threaten logistics routes and investor confidence.

250.s: Political and fiscal instability with recurring social unrest.
i: Protests and strikes are a recurring risk for operations and travel.
Fragile governments struggle to pass budgets that reduce the deficit.
High oil prices feed through to transport and industry.
250.b: Strikes and protests can disrupt transport and operations at short notice.

268.s: Political crisis and a frozen EU path.
i: Opposition groups and protesters reject the government’s legitimacy.
Moscow’s influence has grown as Western ties cooled.
Membership talks are suspended, and Western sanctions target officials.
268.b: Political tension and frozen EU accession raise uncertainty for investors and transit trade.

275.s: Gaza faces a humanitarian emergency and unresolved governance; the West Bank is volatile.
i: Reconstruction is barely under way and access for aid remains restricted.
Security arrangements and the future administration of Gaza remain unsettled.
Military raids and settler attacks keep the territory on edge.
275.b: Restricted access and destruction make commercial activity in Gaza close to impossible.

276.s: Stable, but industry is under pressure from energy costs.
i: Manufacturers face high energy prices and weak export demand.
Sabotage, drone sightings over bases and cyber activity continue.
A strong far right complicates coalition politics.
276.b: Industrial firms face high energy costs and weak export demand.

304.s: A focus of US strategic pressure in the Arctic.
i: Washington’s push for control strains ties with Denmark.
Great-power interest is bringing more military activity.
Rare earth projects attract competing foreign investors.
304.b: Mining investors face geopolitical scrutiny as the US, China and Europe compete for critical minerals.

332.s: Gangs control most of the capital.
i: Gangs hold most of Port-au-Prince and key roads.
The UN-backed Gang Suppression Force is still building up.
Over a million people are displaced, and hunger is widespread.
332.b: Gang control of roads and ports makes operations and the movement of goods extremely dangerous.

356.s: Strong growth, but highly exposed to the Gulf war through energy and its workers there.
i: India imports most of its oil, and millions of Indians, many from Kerala, work in Gulf states within range of strikes. An Indian seafarer was killed in an attack near Oman in early November.
Relations remain hostile after the 2025 conflict, and another attack could trigger a crisis.
On 5 November the US sanctioned Indian and Turkish firms accused of helping Iranian tankers, including an Indian couple accused of faking ship registries.
356.b: High oil prices raise import costs, while Gulf disruption threatens remittances and US sanctions add compliance risk for traders.

360.s: Fiscal and social pressures in a large, stable democracy.
i: Anger over spending and privileges sparked mass protests in 2025.
High oil prices make subsidies expensive.
Chinese vessels contest waters near Natuna.
360.b: Fuel subsidy costs and protest risk weigh on policy, while nickel and palm oil exports remain strong.

364.s: At war with the US and Israel since 28 February. Washington is tightening its blockade while Qatar pushes a plan to reopen Hormuz.
i: On 7 November US forces disabled a cargo ship trying to breach the blockade and launched a task force to cut Iran’s land supply routes, following new strikes on Qeshm Island.
Iran has attacked eight vessels in and around the strait since 1 November, and the UN counts 25 seafarers killed in Hormuz incidents since the war began.
Qatar has put forward a plan to reopen the strait as part of ending the war, but no agreement has been announced.
src: Al Jazeera: US launches task force to disrupt Iran’s land supply routes (8 Nov)
Seatrade Maritime: Crew abandon tanker in Hormuz, US strikes bulker (8 Nov)
ABC News: Explosions heard in Strait of Hormuz as Iran reviews proposals (8 Nov)
364.b: Sanctions make almost all business with Iran unlawful for Western firms, and the war threatens all Gulf shipping and energy flows.
sc: Grinding stalemate: the blockade and tit-for-tat strikes continue, and Hormuz stays largely shut while Qatari-led talks drag on.
Major escalation: a large US strike campaign before the new Congress sits in January, met by Iranian attacks on Gulf states and shipping.
Framework deal: Iran halts attacks on shipping and the US eases its blockade, so Hormuz traffic begins to recover.

368.s: A battleground between Iran-aligned militias and the US.
i: New Iran-aligned groups formed in 2026 have joined attacks on US and allied targets.
Iran has struck targets in the Kurdistan Region, which hosts foreign firms and US personnel.
Export disruption and sanctions enforcement put salaries and the federal budget under strain.
368.b: Militia attacks threaten staff and oil operations, especially in the Kurdistan Region.

376.s: Engaged on several fronts, with no clear winner from the 27 October election.
i: Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran. A new exchange would bring Iranian missile fire back onto Israeli cities and infrastructure.
The IDF is striking in Lebanon again while Iran is reported to have raised Hezbollah’s readiness.
Likud came first on 27 October, but neither bloc has a clear Knesset majority. Coalition talks will set policy on Iran, Lebanon and Gaza.
376.b: Missile threats and reserve call-ups disrupt staffing, and the tech sector faces war-related uncertainty.

392.s: Rising friction with China and heavy dependence on Gulf energy.
i: Beijing demanded in September that Tokyo correct its stance on Taiwan.
Most of Japan’s crude passes through Hormuz.
Launches over or near Japan remain possible.
392.b: Most of Japan’s crude passes through Hormuz, so energy-intensive industries face rising costs.

400.s: Squeezed between regional wars, with US staff being reduced.
i: Missiles and drones crossing Jordanian airspace create risk of debris and stray strikes.
Washington is moving some diplomats and families out as escalation fears grow.
Weak growth, high unemployment and large refugee populations limit room for shocks.
400.b: Regional conflict deters tourism and investment, though Jordan remains a relatively stable base.

404.s: Youth protests and debt ahead of the 2027 election.
i: Youth-led protests over taxes and police violence turn deadly.
Debt servicing absorbs much of government revenue.
404.b: Protests and debt pressure affect operations in Nairobi and investor sentiment.

408.s: Deepening military ties with Russia and an expanding weapons programme.
i: Troops and munitions sent to Russia bring cash and technology in return.
Testing and production continue with few constraints.
Sanctions enforcement has weakened as UN monitoring lapsed.
408.b: Sanctions prohibit almost all business, and missile tests affect regional markets.

410.s: Stable, with North Korea and energy imports as the main exposures.
i: Pyongyang’s ties with Moscow raise the military stakes on the peninsula.
High oil and LNG prices hit a trade-dependent economy.
US tariffs and burden-sharing demands strain planning.
410.b: High energy import costs and US trade policy weigh on manufacturers.

414.s: Within range of Iranian and Iraqi militia strikes, and almost wholly dependent on Gulf shipping.
i: Strikes from Iran and Iraqi militias
Kuwait has been hit during the war, including by new Iran-aligned Iraqi groups.
Kuwait has no pipeline bypass, so its oil exports rise and fall with the strait.
Bases hosting US forces remain on Iran’s stated target list.
414.b: Oil exports depend entirely on Hormuz, and staff face strike risk.

422.s: Caught between Israeli strikes and Hezbollah’s ties to Iran, with a weak state in the middle.
i: Israeli strikes continue in the south, and Israel has reportedly drawn up plans to occupy Tyre, Sidon and Nabatieh if Hezbollah joins a renewed Iran war.
President Joseph Aoun’s government is under US pressure over seized explosives and the group’s wider arsenal.
The banking crisis is unresolved and reconstruction money is stalled by the security situation.
422.b: Banking collapse and the risk of renewed war make operations extremely difficult.

434.s: Divided between rival governments and armed groups.
i: East and west remain under separate authorities.
Fighting between armed groups breaks out with little warning.
Production can be shut in as political leverage.
434.b: Oil production can be shut in for political leverage, and militia clashes threaten staff.

466.s: Jihadist pressure has reached the capital’s supply lines.
i: Blockades of fuel convoys have caused shortages in Bamako.
The junta relies on Russia’s Africa Corps and has dissolved political parties.
Foreign workers, including miners, are targeted for ransom.
466.b: Fuel blockades, kidnapping and military rule make mining and logistics high risk.

484.s: Cartel violence and pressure from Washington.
i: Extortion, cargo theft and homicide remain high in many states.
Cartel terrorist designations raise the risk of unilateral US action.
The 2026 trade review keeps North American supply chains uncertain.
484.b: Cartel extortion and cargo theft raise logistics costs, and the USMCA review clouds nearshoring plans.

498.s: A frontline neighbour exposed to spillover and hybrid pressure.
i: At least five Russian weapons, including missiles and drones, exploded on Moldovan territory in early October.
Disinformation and covert funding target the pro-EU government.
Winter supply and prices remain a vulnerability.
498.b: War spillover and hybrid interference raise risks for investors and energy supply.

512.s: Outside the fighting but close to the shipping lanes where it happens.
i: Ships keep being hit in Omani waters near Hormuz. An attack there in early November killed an Indian seafarer.
Muscat remains a quiet go-between for Washington and Tehran.
High prices help in the short term, but diversification is slow.
512.b: Ports and shipping near Hormuz face attack risk, though Oman remains a relatively stable base.

562.s: Military rule and insurgency on several borders.
i: Attacks in the Tillabéri and Diffa regions are frequent.
The junta has cut ties with Western partners and ECOWAS.
Disputes over uranium and oil assets deter investors.
562.b: Resource nationalism and insurgency threaten uranium and oil investors.

566.s: Widespread insecurity in an economy under reform.
i: Mass kidnappings and attacks continue across the north and centre.
Friction with the US over security
Washington has pressed Abuja over attacks on Christians.
Subsidy and currency reforms keep living costs high.
566.b: Kidnapping and insecurity raise costs for staff and logistics, and currency volatility affects importers.

586.s: Militancy on two fronts and lasting hostility with India.
i: Attacks on security forces and Chinese-linked projects continue.
Clashes with the Taliban government have flared over cross-border militants.
Any major attack in India risks another military exchange.
586.b: Militancy threatens staff and Chinese-linked projects, and border clashes disrupt trade.

i: A new government took office in July after a fragmented election.
Extortion and illegal gold mining are spreading.
Mining regions are prone to road blockades.
604.b: Political volatility and illegal mining affect copper and gold operations.

608.s: On the front line of the South China Sea.
i: Chinese coast guard ships regularly block and ram Philippine vessels.
Rivalry between the two dynasties destabilises politics.
A strong El Niño and typhoons threaten crops and infrastructure.
608.b: South China Sea incidents threaten fishing and shipping, and typhoons disrupt supply chains.

616.s: NATO’s eastern hub, targeted by sabotage and airspace incursions.
i: Russian-linked sabotage and drones crossing the border test Polish defences.
Organised migration across the Belarus border remains a flashpoint.
Record defence spending brings opportunity and procurement strain.
616.b: Sabotage risk and border tension affect logistics, while defence spending creates opportunities.

634.s: Hosts the largest US air base in the region and ships almost all its LNG through Hormuz.
i: Al Udeid makes Qatar a likely target if strikes on Iran resume. The US is drawing down embassy staff.
The Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck en route to Pakistan in early November, and Hormuz remains effectively shut.
Doha’s channels to Tehran and Washington give it leverage, and some protection.
634.b: LNG exports through Hormuz are at risk, with global consequences for gas buyers.

642.s: Exposed to Black Sea spillover and fiscal strain.
i: Drone debris and attacks on shipping near its waters are recurring.
The EU’s largest deficit forces unpopular tax and spending changes.
Nationalist parties remain strong after a disputed election cycle.
642.b: Black Sea security and fiscal tightening affect investors and traders.

643.s: Waging war in Ukraine while absorbing long-range drone strikes on its energy sector.
i: Ukrainian drones set the Afipsky oil refinery in Krasnodar Krai on fire on 6 November, the latest in a sustained campaign against Russia’s oil sector.
European navies are seizing shadow-fleet tankers, raising the cost of moving Russian oil.
Officials are working to calm fears of fuel shortages at home.
643.b: Sanctions make most business with Russia unlawful, and drone strikes disrupt its energy exports.

682.s: A co-belligerent against Iran, absorbing drone and missile fire while oil prices run high.
i: Air defences intercepted threats near Riyadh, Al Kharj, Khamis Mushait and Medina in mid-October.
Escalation in Yemen keeps the kingdom’s western shipping lanes under threat.
Brent above $100 lifts revenue, but rerouting exports by pipeline concentrates risk on a few assets.
682.b: Drone and missile threats raise security costs for staff and energy infrastructure.

688.s: A student-led list won a parliamentary majority on 25 October, ending Aleksandar Vučić’s long dominance.
i: Vučić conceded after the Student List won about 54% of the vote. Forming a government from a new, untested movement will take time.
Tensions in northern Kosovo can flare quickly, and a new government’s approach is not yet known.
A new government may shift Belgrade’s balance between the EU and Russia, with knock-on effects for energy deals and EU accession.
688.b: A new government may reshape investment rules and energy deals.

706.s: Insurgency and disputed politics around the Horn of Africa.
i: The group has retaken ground and still strikes Mogadishu.
Disagreement over the electoral model strains federal–state relations.
Competition over ports and recognition draws in outside powers.
706.b: Al-Shabaab attacks threaten staff and port operations.

710.s: Stable coalition politics with infrastructure and trade pressures.
i: Ports, rail and power remain constraints on growth.
Diplomatic tension with Washington hits trade preferences.
Municipal elections test the coalition government.
710.b: Port, rail and power constraints raise costs, and US trade tension affects exporters.

728.s: At risk of sliding back into civil war.
i: The prosecution of First Vice President Riek Machar has fractured the peace deal.
Exports through war-torn Sudan are repeatedly disrupted.
Refugees from Sudan add pressure to an already stretched aid system.
728.b: Oil exports through Sudan are repeatedly disrupted, and the risk of conflict is high.

729.s: The world’s largest humanitarian crisis, driven by the war between the army and the RSF.
i: Fighting has shifted to Kordofan after the RSF captured El Fasher in 2025.
Famine conditions affect several regions, and aid access is blocked.
External support to both sides prolongs the war and risks regional spillover.
729.b: War and famine make commercial operations impossible in most of the country.

760.s: A fragile post-Assad transition with violence at the margins.
i: The transitional government’s authority is uneven outside major cities.
Clashes involving Alawite, Druze and Kurdish communities keep recurring.
Israeli strikes and ground activity in southern Syria continue.
760.b: Sanctions relief is partial, and insecurity limits investment.

784.s: High exposure to Iranian retaliation as a host of US operations and a Gulf business hub.
i: The IRGC has named states hosting US bases as targets. The US is cutting staff at its UAE posts.
Shipping attacks near Hormuz threaten ports, bunkering and energy exports.
Aviation disruption, expatriate staffing and insurance costs are rising for firms based in Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
784.b: Drone and missile risk and Hormuz disruption threaten aviation, ports and business continuity.

792.s: A regional pivot exposed to wars on two sides.
i: A Turkish-owned grain ship was sunk by Russian drones on 5 October.
Border security, energy prices and refugee flows are all at risk.
High inflation and tight policy weigh on businesses.
src: United Nations: COP31 in Antalya, 9–20 November 2026
792.b: Black Sea shipping risk and inflation affect traders and manufacturers.

804.s: Entering a fifth winter of full-scale war, with the grid under heavy attack and new peace talks expected in Abu Dhabi.
i: DTEK counted 78 Russian strikes on energy sites in three days, bringing rolling blackouts, and ballistic missiles hit Kyiv in several waves overnight on 6–7 November.
Russian forces lost ground in October for the second month running, after Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi disrupted the push on Donetsk’s fortress belt.
Washington and the Kremlin have both confirmed US-mediated talks with Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November, though earlier rounds have not produced a ceasefire.
src: Meduza: Trilateral talks set for 10–11 November in Abu Dhabi (3 Nov)
Naharnet: Kremlin confirms Abu Dhabi talks (3 Nov)
804.b: Strikes on the grid disrupt operations, though reconstruction and defence contracts create opportunities.
sc: Talks continue without a ceasefire; Russia keeps striking the grid through winter and the front moves little.
Talks collapse and Russia intensifies winter strikes, causing prolonged blackouts and new displacement.
An energy-infrastructure truce or major prisoner exchange holds, opening the way to leader-level talks.

i: Red Sea insecurity keeps Suez Canal traffic and income depressed.
High external debt leaves little room for new shocks.
Both conflicts push refugees and security risks toward Egypt.
818.b: Lost Suez Canal revenue and currency pressure raise costs for importers and investors.

826.s: Stable, with energy prices and hybrid threats as the main pressures.
i: Oil above $100 pushes up inflation and household bills.
Sabotage, cyber attacks and espionage are a persistent threat.
Tight fiscal room limits defence and public-service spending.
826.b: High energy prices raise costs, but the business environment remains stable.

840.s: A party to the Iran war, now facing a Congress under Democratic control.
i: Trump confirmed new strikes on Iran on 6 November, and the US has warned Americans across the Middle East of a heightened threat of armed attacks.
Democrats won both the House and Senate on 3 November, as called by CBS News and NBC News, setting up clashes with the White House over war powers, budgets and trade.
Tariffs and frequent policy shifts keep supply chains uncertain for partners.
840.b: Tariff shifts and Iran war decisions create uncertainty for trading partners and energy markets.

854.s: Much of the country is outside state control.
i: JNIM and Islamic State affiliates contest large parts of the territory.
The junta has suppressed critics and conscripted dissenters.
Around two million people have been displaced.
854.b: Insecurity puts staff and mining operations at serious risk outside the capital.

862.s: A transition run under US oversight after Maduro’s capture.
i: US forces captured Nicolás Maduro on 3 January. Acting President Delcy Rodríguez governs with US backing.
US control over exports reshapes contracts and sanctions exposure.
There is no agreed timeline for free elections, and repression continues.
862.b: US control of oil exports reshapes contracts, and sanctions exposure remains complex.

887.s: The civil war has escalated alongside the Iran war, and the Bab al-Mandab is contested again.
i: Houthi missiles hit Aden and Marib in October, striking areas held by the internationally recognised government.
Red Sea transit remains one of the riskiest commercial routes in the world.
Food insecurity is deepening as fighting and funding cuts disrupt aid.
887.b: Houthi attacks make Red Sea shipping one of the riskiest routes in the world.

004.s: Humanitarian strain, extremist groups and conflict with Pakistan.
i: Mass returns from Pakistan and Iran meet shrinking aid budgets.
Border fighting has disrupted trade crossings.
The group remains capable of attacks at home and abroad.
004.b: Sanctions on the Taliban government and insecurity make commercial activity close to impossible beyond humanitarian work.

050.s: A political transition under economic pressure.
i: The post-Hasina order is still settling after this year’s election.
High fuel prices strain reserves and power supply.
Over a million refugees depend on shrinking aid.
050.b: Garment exporters face higher fuel costs and political uncertainty that can disrupt production.

076.s: Lula won a fourth term, but his opponent has not conceded.
i: Lula beat Flávio Bolsonaro in the 25 October runoff with about 52% of the vote. Bolsonaro says he will seek annulment, though his own Liberal Party recognised the result.
Tariffs and political disputes with Washington hit exporters.
Spending pressures test the fiscal framework.
076.b: A large consumer market with an uncertain political outlook; US tariffs hit exporters of coffee, steel and agricultural goods.

032.s: Deep reform with currency and social risks.
i: Low reserves keep the peso exposed.
032.b: Reforms are opening up energy and mining, but currency controls and volatility complicate repatriating profits.

036.s: Stable, with fuel security as a weak point.
i: Australia imports most of its fuel and holds low reserves.
Trade has stabilised, but security tensions persist.
China and Australia compete for influence among Pacific island states.
036.b: A stable market, but low fuel reserves make transport and logistics vulnerable to Gulf supply shocks.

380.s: A stable government, with energy costs and public debt as the main pressures.
i: High oil and gas prices from the Gulf war push up costs for households and industry.
One of Europe’s highest debt burdens leaves little room for new spending.
Arrivals from North Africa remain a recurring political flashpoint.
380.b: Energy-intensive manufacturers face rising costs from high oil and gas prices.

724.s: A strong economy run by a minority government that relies on smaller parties.
i: The government depends on regional and smaller parties to pass laws and budgets.
Inquiries touching figures close to the government weigh on politics.
Higher fuel prices raise costs for transport and a tourism-dependent economy.
724.b: Higher fuel costs affect transport and tourism, though the economy remains resilient.

528.s: Stable, but exposed to shipping disruption and fragmented coalition politics.
i: Fragmented results make coalition building slow and governments fragile.
Europe’s largest port feels the knock-on effects of Red Sea and Gulf disruption.
North Sea cables and pipelines are potential targets for hybrid attacks.
528.b: Rotterdam’s port and logistics firms feel the effects of global shipping disruption.

056.s: Home to EU institutions and most frozen Russian assets, and a target for hybrid activity.
i: Repeated drone sightings over airports and military sites since 2025 have disrupted flights.
Euroclear in Brussels holds most frozen Russian central bank assets, putting Belgium at the centre of EU decisions on them.
High deficits force difficult budget negotiations.
056.b: Brussels-based firms face little direct risk, but airport disruption from drone sightings can affect travel and logistics.

752.s: A new NATO member facing criminal violence at home and tension in the Baltic.
i: Shootings and bombings linked to criminal networks remain a national security priority.
Damage to undersea cables and Russian activity keep the Baltic tense.
Sweden is expanding defence spending and Baltic patrols.
752.b: Gang violence and Baltic security risks require strong security planning.

578.s: Low risk, with a growing role as Europe’s gas supplier.
i: With Gulf LNG disrupted, Norwegian gas matters more to Europe, and so does the security of its fields and pipelines.
Russian military activity near the shared Arctic border is rising.
Energy platforms and subsea links are potential hybrid targets.
578.b: Norwegian gas is more valuable to Europe, making offshore infrastructure security a priority.

246.s: A frontline NATO state on Russia’s border.
i: Finland’s eastern border crossings have been closed since late 2023 over migrant pressure attributed to Moscow.
Cable and pipeline damage in the Gulf of Finland has been linked to Russian-connected vessels.
Sluggish growth and high unemployment strain public finances.
246.b: Closed eastern border crossings and Baltic cable risks affect logistics and telecoms.

208.s: A close US ally strained by Washington’s push over Greenland.
i: Washington’s push for control of Greenland strains relations within NATO.
Drones over airports and military bases in 2025 led Copenhagen to describe them as a hybrid attack.
Russian shadow-fleet tankers pass through Danish waters, raising security and spill risks.
208.b: Danish shipping and energy firms are exposed to Baltic security risks and US–Denmark tensions over Greenland.

300.s: Stable, with heavy exposure to global shipping risk.
i: Greek owners control a large share of the world’s tanker fleet, which is exposed to Gulf and Red Sea attacks.
Maritime disputes in the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean can flare.
Sea arrivals from Libya and Türkiye remain a pressure point.
300.b: Greek-owned shipping faces high war-risk insurance costs in the Gulf and Red Sea.

348.s: Péter Magyar’s government is unwinding 16 years of Orbán rule after an April landslide.
i: Hungary still relies heavily on Russian oil and gas, leaving it exposed to sanctions and supply shocks.
With a two-thirds majority, the Tisza government can rewrite laws, but dismantling entrenched networks will take time.
Unlocking frozen EU funds depends on anti-corruption and rule-of-law reforms.
src: RFE/RL: Magyar scores landslide win to oust Orbán
348.b: Reforms could unlock EU funds and investor confidence, though Russian energy dependence remains a supply risk.

203.s: Stable, with a populist-led government recalibrating foreign policy.
i: The government has signalled a cooler line on aid to Ukraine than its predecessor.
High energy prices weigh on a manufacturing-heavy economy.
Sabotage and disinformation campaigns remain a security concern.
203.b: Manufacturers face high energy costs, while policy shifts on Ukraine may affect defence-sector contracts.

040.s: Stable, but with a weak economy and a strong far right.
i: Industry has struggled with high energy costs and soft export demand.
The FPÖ remains a powerful force in national politics.
Ending reliance on Russian gas has raised costs and supply questions.
040.b: High energy costs weigh on manufacturers and suppliers to German industry.

756.s: Low risk, with trade and sanctions compliance the main issues.
i: US tariffs have hit Swiss exporters, from watches to machinery.
Banks and commodity traders face scrutiny over Russian and Iranian sanctions.
Safe-haven inflows lift the currency and squeeze exporters.
756.b: US tariffs hit exporters, and banks and traders face sanctions compliance scrutiny.

620.s: Low risk, though politics has become more fragmented.
i: Repeated elections and a rising populist right make governments less stable.
High rents and property prices drive public frustration.
Higher oil prices feed through to transport and inflation.
620.b: Low risk, with high fuel prices the main cost pressure.

372.s: Low risk, but highly exposed to US trade and investment.
i: Heavy reliance on US pharmaceutical and tech firms leaves Ireland exposed to US trade policy.
Transatlantic data cables off Ireland are a potential hybrid target.
A severe shortage of homes is the top domestic political issue.
372.b: US tariff decisions on pharmaceuticals and tech put Ireland’s investment model at risk.

440.s: A NATO frontline state facing repeated hybrid pressure from Belarus.
i: Smuggling balloons from Belarus have repeatedly forced Vilnius airport to close.
Sabotage, cyber attacks and disinformation target Lithuania regularly.
The narrow land corridor to Poland is NATO’s most exposed chokepoint.
440.b: Airport closures and hybrid threats can disrupt logistics and travel.

428.s: A NATO frontline state on Russia’s border.
i: Migrant pushes from Belarus and Russian provocations keep the eastern border tense.
Damage to undersea cables has been linked to Russian-connected vessels.
Relations with the large Russian-speaking minority remain politically sensitive.
428.b: Low commercial risk, but Baltic infrastructure and border security need monitoring.

233.s: A NATO frontline state tested by Russian military provocations.
i: Russian fighter jets entered Estonian airspace in 2025, prompting NATO consultations.
The border city with Russia is a focus of Moscow’s pressure.
Estonia remains a frequent target of Russian-linked cyber operations.
233.b: Low commercial risk, though cyber attacks and Russian provocations require strong security planning.

051.s: Pashinyan’s party won a majority in June, backing a US-brokered peace process with Azerbaijan.
i: A framework agreed in Washington in 2025 has yet to be fully implemented.
Moscow is using economic levers as Yerevan turns towards the West.
Opposition parties and church figures dispute the government’s direction.
src: JAMnews: Final election results, Pashinyan’s party wins majority
051.b: A peace deal could open new transport routes between Europe and Asia, though Russian economic pressure is a risk for investors.

031.s: Gaining from the peace process but bordering Iran at war.
i: A long border with Iran exposes Azerbaijan to refugee flows, airspace risks and strikes.
Relations with Moscow have soured sharply since 2025.
A US-brokered framework offers stability, but implementation is incomplete.
031.b: Oil and gas exports are steady, but proximity to the Iran war raises security and insurance costs.

398.s: Stable, but its oil exports depend on a pipeline through Russia.
i: Most exports flow via the CPC pipeline to Novorossiysk, where Ukrainian drone strikes have disrupted operations.
Trade with Russia brings the risk of Western secondary sanctions.
Power remains concentrated, with limited space for opposition.
398.b: Oil exporters depend on a pipeline through Russia that has been disrupted by drone strikes.

144.s: Recovering from its 2022 default, now squeezed by high fuel prices.
i: The recovery depends on sticking to an IMF programme and restructured debt terms.
Oil above $100 strains reserves and revives memories of 2022 shortages.
Rebuilding after severe cyclone damage in late 2025 strains the budget.
144.b: High fuel prices strain reserves and import capacity.

524.s: Balendra Shah’s government, elected in a March landslide after the 2025 Gen Z uprising, is under pressure to deliver.
i: High expectations of the new government
The RSP won nearly two-thirds of seats and must show fast results on corruption and jobs.
Youth unemployment drives mass migration, and Gulf remittances are exposed to the Iran war.
The new government must manage pressure from both neighbours.
src: The Jakarta Post: Ex-rapper’s party wins Nepal election in landslide (13 Mar)
524.b: Gulf remittance flows and a new government’s reform agenda shape the economic outlook.

764.s: Political instability and a tense border with Cambodia.
i: Deadly clashes in 2025 left the border fragile despite a ceasefire.
Frequent changes of prime minister and court interventions unsettle policy.
High household debt and soft tourism weigh on the economy.
764.b: Border tension with Cambodia and political instability affect tourism and investment.

704.s: A manufacturing hub exposed to US trade policy.
i: Heavy dependence on exports to the US leaves Vietnam exposed to tariff decisions.
Disputes with China over islands and fishing grounds continue.
Sweeping investigations can slow approvals and unsettle investors.
704.b: Exporters depend heavily on the US market, so tariff decisions drive risk.

458.s: Stable, with exposure to tech trade and the South China Sea.
i: US export controls and tariffs affect Malaysia’s large chip-packaging sector.
Chinese vessels operate near Malaysian oil and gas fields.
The governing coalition holds together, but tensions persist.
458.b: Semiconductor packaging firms face US export controls and tariff risk.

554.s: Low risk, with distance from conflict but exposure to fuel and trade.
i: Almost all fuel is imported, so high oil prices feed straight into costs.
China is the largest export market, which creates political and economic exposure.
China and Western partners compete for influence across the Pacific.
554.b: High fuel prices raise transport and agricultural costs.

152.s: A stable democracy with a new government focused on crime.
i: Transnational gangs have driven a rise in violent crime.
Mining rules and royalties matter greatly to investors.
Inequality and protest risk remain after the 2019 unrest.
152.b: Copper and lithium producers benefit from demand, but crime and mining-policy shifts affect costs.

068.s: A deep economic crisis under a new government pushing painful reforms.
i: Fuel and dollar shortages, high inflation and low reserves strain the economy.
The government that took office in November 2025 is pushing reforms, including cuts to fuel subsidies.
Road blockades by unions and political groups frequently disrupt trade.
068.b: Fuel and dollar shortages, blockades and policy shifts make operations and payments unpredictable.

012.s: A gas supplier with unsettled borders.
i: Instability in Mali and Niger threatens Algeria’s long southern border.
Higher demand for its gas raises Algeria’s importance to Europe.
Relations with Morocco and France remain tense.
012.b: Europe’s need for non-Russian gas raises Algeria’s value as a supplier, but state control limits foreign investment.

504.s: Stable, with youth discontent and Western Sahara diplomacy in focus.
i: Gen Z-led protests over health and education spending erupted in 2025.
A 2025 UN Security Council resolution backed Morocco’s autonomy plan, but the dispute is not settled.
Prolonged drought threatens agriculture and rural jobs.
504.b: A stable base for manufacturing and exports, though youth protests signal social pressure.

i: Critics, journalists and opposition figures face arrest and prosecution.
Weak finances have led to periodic shortages of basic goods.
Tunisia remains a key departure point for boats to Europe.
788.b: Repression and shortages raise operational and reputational risk.

288.s: A stable democracy rebuilding after a debt crisis.
i: Galamsey mining pollutes rivers and fuels local conflict.
Recovery depends on fiscal discipline after the 2022 default.
Jihadist activity in neighbouring Burkina Faso threatens the north.
288.b: Gold and cocoa exporters face illegal mining, debt pressure and northern security risks.

508.s: An insurgency in the north and a fragile political settlement.
i: Islamic State-linked fighters still attack villages and roads in the north.
Major gas projects are restarting, but depend on security improving.
Deadly unrest followed the disputed 2024 election.
508.b: Gas projects in the north depend on security improving in Cabo Delgado.

834.s: Political repression after a violent election.
i: Security forces killed protesters after the disputed October 2025 election.
Opposition leaders face arrest and restrictions.
Unrest and policy uncertainty weigh on investors.
834.b: Political repression and unrest weigh on investor confidence.

events.text: The UN climate conference in Türkiye, with world leaders attending on 11–12 November.

events.text: US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia, confirmed by Washington and the Kremlin.

events.title: APEC leaders’ meeting, Shenzhen
events.text: Asia-Pacific leaders meet in China amid tariff and tech tensions.

events.title: G20 leaders’ summit, Miami
events.text: The first G20 summit hosted by the US, with trade and the Iran war likely on the agenda.

events.title: South Sudan general election (scheduled)
events.text: A long-delayed vote that could test the fragile peace deal.

events.title: New US Congress takes office
events.text: Democrats take control of both chambers, with war powers and budgets in focus.

US strike on Qeshm Island; Hormuz effectively closed.
No clear majority after the 27 October election.
Lula won the presidential runoff; his opponent has not conceded.
